def: A random variable assigns a numerical value to each outcome of a random experiment. It is discrete if it takes only countable (separate) values, and continuous if it can take any value in an interval.
points: A random variable X is a function from the sample space to real numbers.
Discrete random variable: takes finite or countably infinite values, like number of heads in 3 tosses (0, 1, 2, 3).
Continuous random variable: takes any value in an interval, like height or time, measured on a continuous scale.
Discrete variables use a probability mass function (p.m.f.); continuous variables use a probability density function (p.d.f.).
Sum of all probabilities for a discrete variable is always 1; for continuous, the total area under the density curve is 1.
formula: Sum of P(X = xi) = 1  (discrete)     Integral of f(x) dx over all x = 1  (continuous)

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["Random Variable X"] --> B["Discrete: countable values"]
  A --> C["Continuous: any value in interval"]
  B --> D["Uses p.m.f."]
  C --> E["Uses p.d.f."]

example: Tossing 2 coins, let X = number of heads. X can be 0, 1, or 2, so X is a discrete random variable.
tip: Always state clearly whether the variable is discrete or continuous before writing its distribution table — examiners check this definition step.

def: A probability mass function gives the probability that a discrete random variable X takes each specific value xi, written P(X = xi).
points: List all possible values x1, x2, ..., xn of the discrete random variable.
For each value, find P(X = xi), the probability of that outcome.
Every probability must satisfy 0 <= P(X = xi) <= 1.
The sum of all probabilities must equal 1: sum P(X = xi) = 1.
Usually presented as a table with values of X in one row and probabilities in the next.
Used to answer questions like P(X <= 2) by adding relevant probabilities.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["List values x1 to xn"] --> B["Assign probability to each"]
  B --> C["Check each probability between 0 and 1"]
  C --> D["Check sum equals 1"]

example: X: 0, 1, 2 with P(X=0)=0.25, P(X=1)=0.5, P(X=2)=0.25. Sum = 1, so this is a valid p.m.f.
tip: Before solving any problem, always verify the sum of given probabilities equals 1 — this check carries marks and catches errors early.

def: A probability density function f(x) describes the relative likelihood of a continuous random variable taking values near a point x; probability over an interval is found using integration.
points: f(x) must satisfy f(x) >= 0 for all x in its domain.
Total area under the curve f(x) over the entire range must equal 1.
Probability of X lying between a and b is the definite integral of f(x) dx from a to b.
For a continuous variable, P(X = any single point) = 0, since area under a point is zero.
So P(a < X < b) = P(a <= X <= b) for continuous random variables.
f(x) is often given as a piecewise function, defined differently on different intervals, and zero elsewhere.
formula: integral of f(x) dx over domain = 1     P(a<X<b) = integral from a to b of f(x) dx

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Given f(x)"] --> B["Check f(x) >= 0"]
  B --> C["Check total area = 1"]
  C --> D["Integrate over a,b for P(a<X<b)"]

example: f(x) = 2x for 0 < x < 1, else 0. Check: integral of 2x dx from 0 to 1 = [x^2] from 0 to 1 = 1. Valid p.d.f. P(0<X<0.5) = [x^2] from 0 to 0.5 = 0.25.
tip: Always first verify total area equals 1 before using f(x) to find any probability or constant k.

def: Expectation E(X), or mean, gives the average value a random variable takes in the long run. Variance Var(X) measures how spread out the values are around the mean.
points: For discrete X: E(X) = sum of xi . P(X = xi), over all values.
For continuous X: E(X) = integral of x . f(x) dx over the domain.
E(X^2) is found similarly, using xi^2 . P(X=xi) or x^2 . f(x) dx.
Variance formula: Var(X) = E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2.
Standard deviation is the square root of variance: SD = sqrt(Var(X)).
Larger variance means values are more spread out from the mean.
formula: E(X) = sum xi P(X=xi)     Var(X) = E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Find E(X)"] --> C["Find E(X^2)"]
  B["Distribution table"] --> A
  B --> C
  C --> D["Var(X) = E(X^2) - E(X)^2"]

tip: Always compute E(X^2) as a separate step before using the variance formula — combining steps often causes calculation errors.

def: The cumulative distribution function (c.d.f.), F(x), gives the probability that the random variable X takes a value less than or equal to x, that is F(x) = P(X <= x).
points: For discrete X, F(x) is found by adding up all P(X = xi) for xi <= x.
For continuous X, F(x) is found by integrating f(t) from the lowest value up to x.
F(x) is non-decreasing: it never goes down as x increases.
F(x) ranges from 0 (at the smallest value) to 1 (at the largest value).
For continuous variables, f(x) = dF(x)/dx, so the p.d.f. is the derivative of the c.d.f.
Used to directly find probabilities like P(X <= a) without separately summing or integrating each time.
formula: F(x) = P(X <= x)     f(x) = dF(x)/dx (continuous case)

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Given p.m.f. or p.d.f."] --> B["Sum or integrate up to x"]
  B --> C["Get F(x) = P(X <= x)"]
  C --> D["Use for probability questions"]

tip: Remember F(x) always starts near 0 and ends at exactly 1 — use this to check your working at the final value.

t: Finding the Constant k in a Distribution
def: When a p.m.f. or p.d.f. is given with an unknown constant k, we use the basic rule that total probability must equal 1 to solve for k.
points: Write out the given p.m.f. table or p.d.f. expression containing k.
For discrete case: set up the equation sum of all P(X = xi) = 1, then solve for k.
For continuous case: set up integral of f(x) dx over the full domain equal to 1, then solve for k.
Solve the resulting algebraic (or integral) equation for k.
Substitute k back into the original distribution to get the complete, valid distribution.
Check that no probability becomes negative or greater than 1 after substituting k.
formula: sum P(X=xi) = 1  or  integral f(x) dx = 1, then solve for k

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Write distribution with k"] --> B["Set total probability = 1"]
  B --> C["Solve equation for k"]
  C --> D["Substitute k back"]
  D --> E["Verify all probabilities valid"]

tip: After finding k, always substitute back and check every probability lies between 0 and 1 — this verification step is often separately awarded a mark.
